# Preface {.unnumbered}

A practical guide to getting work done on **MedicineBow**, the University of Wyoming's
high-performance computing (HPC) cluster, run by the **Advanced Research Computing Center
(ARCC)**.

It is written for people joining the **ASCEND** engine and its **ARID** program, and
assumes you are comfortable on a computer but have never used a shared supercomputer. Each
chapter explains *why* before *how*.

## Why this book exists

The official documentation — the [ARCC wiki](https://pages.arcc.uwyo.edu/arcc-wiki/main/) —
is good but has gaps and is in places out of date. The content here was written while
onboarding on the live cluster and cross-checked against the running system in July 2026.
Where the docs and the machine disagree, this book follows the machine and notes the
conflict.

::: {.callout-note}
## This is not an official ARCC document
It's a community onboarding guide. It can drift out of date, and ARCC can change
policy at any time. When in doubt, the
[official wiki](https://pages.arcc.uwyo.edu/arcc-wiki/main/) and
`arcc-help@uwyo.edu` are authoritative. Corrections are very welcome.
:::

## Quick orientation

1. **You cannot request your own account — your PI must.** No project, no account.
   (See @sec-account.)
2. **Nothing on the cluster is backed up.** Not home, not project, not scratch. There
   are snapshots, but they live on the same array. (See @sec-storage.)
3. **Never run real computation on a login node.** Log in, then hand work to the
   scheduler (Slurm) or grab an interactive session. (See @sec-why-scheduler.)
4. **Every job must name your project account** with `--account=<project>`. (See
   @sec-anatomy.)
5. **The partition and QOS you choose decide how long you wait and how big you can go.**
   Short test runs and long simulations belong in different queues (@sec-partitions,
   @sec-queue-times).

## How the book is organized

The chapters run roughly in the order you'll need them: getting an account and logging in, a
minimal Linux survival kit, the filesystems and moving data, software (modules, conda,
containers), then the bulk of the book on **Slurm** — asking for resources, picking a queue,
watching jobs, arrays, GPUs, and handling preemption and failures. The last few chapters are
quick reference: a cheat sheet, troubleshooting, and a glossary.

Conventions: shell commands you type are shown in `code blocks`. Boxes marked
**Gotcha** or **Important** mark places people reliably get burned.
